entries.title: Kenya’s Ebola cases test preparedness beyond Nairobi
entries.summary: The scare exposed gaps in how far outbreak readiness reaches Kenya’s remote communities.
entries.content:
The scare exposed gaps in how far outbreak readiness reaches Kenya’s remote communities.

Nairobi, Kenya – Kenya’s response to an imported Ebola case has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response in the capital.

But a suspected case in the northeastern county of Wajir has raised a critical question: whether the country’s preparedness measures can protect communities far from major hospitals, laboratories and transport hubs.

The suspected case in Wajir tested negative, according to county officials, easing fears of wider transmission. Yet the incident highlighted the importance of local health facilities being able to recognise suspected infections, isolate patients safely and communicate reliable information to residents.

For communities near Kenya’s borders, preparedness requires more than screening travellers at airports and official crossings.

It also depends on trained health workers, appropriate protective equipment, functioning isolation facilities and clear referral procedures. Residents must know where to seek care and how to respond when health authorities raise the alarm.

Wajir’s readiness under scrutiny

Garad Saney Mohamed, communications director for Wajir county, told Al Jazeera that the county had established an isolation centre in Wajir town and formed a rapid response team to strengthen its preparedness.

He said the county was also using radio campaigns, community health promoters, school health programmes and posters to raise awareness about Ebola. A preparedness plan and budget had been put in place, he added.

However, the county did not provide details on the isolation centre’s capacity, the number of health workers trained specifically in Ebola response or the budget allocated to these efforts. Without that information, it is difficult to assess whether the county has the personnel and resources needed to manage suspected infections safely or respond to a wider outbreak.

The suspected case involved a 20-year-old man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda before reaching his home in Wajir on September 20. He was assessed at Habaswein Subcounty Hospital in Wajir South after presenting with a severe febrile illness.

His sample tested negative for Ebola, according to county officials. He was to remain under observation while receiving medical care.

The case prompted precautionary action, but it does not establish whether Wajir’s wider preparedness systems would be sufficient during an outbreak. That would depend on factors including the availability of protective equipment, staff trained in infection prevention and control, safe sample transport and reliable links between local facilities and designated testing laboratories.

Wajir’s proximity to Somalia, which lies 110km (70 miles) to the east, and the movement of people and goods across the border make surveillance and public communication particularly important. Screening at formal entry points remains essential, but it cannot replace the ability of local health facilities and community health workers to recognise warning signs and guide people towards appropriate care.

National screening, local challenges

Kenya’s national response intensified after an Ebola case was linked to a Kenyan travelling from the Democratic Republic of the Congo through Uganda. The patient arrived in Nairobi on October 3, was diagnosed with Bundibugyo virus of the disease and died on October 5, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Kenya notified the WHO on October 6.

The patient had fallen ill while living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and travelled by road to Kampala before flying to Nairobi. Laboratory tests at the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute confirmed the infection, according to the Ministry of Health.

On October 14, Kenya confirmed a second case of Bundibugyo virus disease involving a 39-year-old man who was a close family member of the first patient. He was already in quarantine and under daily monitoring when he developed symptoms, including fever, fatigue and joint pains, on October 13.

Laboratory tests confirmed the infection, and he was transferred to a designated treatment centre for supportive care. The Ministry of Health said the two cases were linked and there was no evidence of transmission in the wider community.

Authorities subsequently intensified surveillance at points of entry, contact tracing and public communication. The negative test result in Wajir underscored the importance of investigating suspected infections promptly and using laboratory testing to establish whether the virus is present.

As of October 6, Kenya had screened 652,584 travellers, tested 267 samples and trained 4,971 healthcare workers in Ebola prevention and management, according to the Ministry of Health.

By October 12, the WHO reported that more than 665,000 travellers had been screened and 127 contacts had been listed, with 94 in quarantine. Five laboratories had been designated to test for the disease, and nearly 5,000 health workers had received training.

These figures demonstrate the scale of the national response. But the number of travellers screened or health workers trained does not, on its own, establish how effectively those resources are distributed or whether individual counties can manage suspected infections.

For Wajir, the key questions concern the readiness of local facilities, the availability of trained personnel and protective equipment, and the speed with which samples can be transported for testing. The county has outlined the measures it has taken, but the available information does not provide a complete picture of its operational capacity.

Preparedness means more than the numbers

Health workers need to recognise suspected cases, follow infection-prevention protocols, collect and transport samples safely, and refer patients without exposing others. Facilities must also have appropriate protective equipment and clear procedures for managing suspected infections.

The WHO reported that Kenya’s national preparedness score rose from 66 percent in May to 82 percent in July. The assessment covered measures including surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and treatment facilities, and trained response teams.

The improvement suggests that preparedness measures had advanced before the imported case was confirmed. However, a national score cannot establish whether every county has the equipment, staffing and referral arrangements needed to respond effectively. Assessments of local capacity are essential to identifying gaps that national figures may not reveal.

The Kenya Red Cross has also supported preparedness and public awareness efforts. Dr Paul Olale, a representative of the organisation, told Al Jazeera about a preparedness assessment. However, the basis of the separate figure attributed to the organisation was not established in the information available for this report, making it difficult to determine what it measured or whether it identified county-level weaknesses.

The organisation has highlighted the need to counter misinformation. During an outbreak, rumours can leave people uncertain about symptoms, how the virus spreads and whether they should seek medical attention.

For residents, information needs to be practical. People should know where to seek care, how to report a suspected illness and what to do while awaiting medical advice. Communication must also address stigma and reassure people that reporting a suspected illness can help protect their families and communities.

Community health promoters, local radio stations, schools and trusted community leaders can help deliver information in languages and formats residents understand. But awareness campaigns are most effective when they are consistent and backed by health services capable of responding promptly to concerns.

Taking preparedness into the community

Wajir’s experience illustrates why Kenya’s Ebola preparedness must be measured not only by national screening figures and training totals, but also by the ability of individual counties to respond safely when a suspected case emerges.

An isolation centre, a rapid response team and public awareness campaigns are important components of an effective response. Their existence alone, however, does not establish whether facilities have adequate equipment, staff can follow established protocols or residents can access reliable information when they need it.

Kenya has demonstrated its ability to mobilise a national response, expand screening and undertake laboratory testing. The challenge is ensuring that these measures translate into effective protection beyond major transport hubs, including in remote communities where access to healthcare and timely information may be more difficult.

Dr Mary Muthoni, Kenya’s principal secretary for public health and professional standards, underscored the importance of protecting frontline staff in remarks delivered on behalf of Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, according to a WHO statement released on October 12.

“No health worker in this country should be asked to attend to a suspected Ebola case without the right protective equipment.”

entries.title: Tunisia: What has Kais Saied achieved economically in seven years?
entries.summary: Rising prices, unemployment and public debt test Saied’s economic promises.
entries.content:
Rising prices, unemployment and public debt test Saied’s economic promises.

For Tunisian taxi driver Houssam Oueslati, inflation has a price tag: The cost of keeping his car on the road.

In 2018, he paid about 35 Tunisian dinars ($13) for engine oil. Today, the same purchase can cost close to 100 dinars ($34). To maintain his income, he has had to work longer hours, spending more of his day behind the wheel to cover rising operating costs.

His experience points to a broader question facing Tunisia nearly seven years into Kais Saied’s presidency: What has changed in the economy, and how much of that change has improved people’s lives?

Saied came to power amid widespread frustration with the political establishment, promising a fairer and more accountable state. Since then, Tunisia has faced the economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, volatile global food and energy prices, and geopolitical turmoil.

These shocks have complicated the country’s recovery, but they do not settle the question of how effectively the government has responded. The economy continues to grow, and overall unemployment has eased from its pandemic-era peak. Yet food prices remain a burden, unemployment among young people is high, and public finances leave the government with limited room to manoeuvre.

For Tunisians such as Oueslati, what matters most is not the headline growth figure but whether their earnings cover the cost of living.

The rising cost of making a living

The price of the engine oil Oueslati buys has increased by approximately 186%, according to figures he provided to Al Jazeera. For a taxi driver, this is not an isolated expense but part of the cost of staying in business.

The pressure extends well beyond transport.

Tunisia’s annual inflation rate reached 5.6% in September 2026, up from 5.4% in August and 4.8% in January, according to the National Institute of Statistics.

Food and beverage prices rose by 8.4% year on year. Poultry prices increased by 16.5%, fruit by 16.3% and lamb by 14.6%. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, stood at 4.9%.

These figures help explain why inflation can remain painful even when its headline rate appears moderate. Inflation measures how quickly prices rise, not whether they are affordable. When prices rise faster than incomes, purchasing power falls. And even when inflation slows, households do not automatically recover what they have lost: Prices generally remain high unless they fall.

Economist Ridha Chkoundali argues that the cumulative effect of price increases is central to understanding the pressure on Tunisian families.

According to his estimates, average annual inflation was 6.8% between 2015 and 2021, compared with 8.1% between 2021 and 2026, indicating stronger inflationary pressures in the latter period.

The government has taken steps to ease the financial pressure. The Central Bank cut its key interest rate twice in 2025, bringing it down to 7%. But lower borrowing costs cannot, alone, restore purchasing power eroded by higher prices.

Chkoundali also argues that tighter access to credit has left consumers with fewer ways to manage expenses. Loans, banking facilities and cheques once allowed some households to spread payments over time, he says. Changes in financing conditions and cheque regulations have narrowed those options.

For families with little savings, essentials now consume more of the household budget, while access to short-term financial support may be more limited.

The challenge is not simply to bring inflation down, but to make everyday life more affordable and give households a chance to rebuild their financial security.

Growth without enough jobs

Tunisia’s economy grew by 2.3% year on year in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics. Growth reached 1.4% compared with the previous quarter.

The 2026 Finance Law had projected annual growth of about 3.3%, setting a more ambitious benchmark for the year.

For Chkoundali, the gap between the budget projection and the quarterly figures highlights a deeper problem: Growth matters to households only when it translates into greater production, investment, employment and income.

The labour market illustrates the challenge.

Tunisia’s overall unemployment rate stood at 14.9% in the second quarter of 2026, down from 15.3% in the same period a year earlier. It had reached 17% in 2020, according to the National Institute of Statistics.

But the headline rate conceals a harsher reality for younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4%, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6%.

For many young people, the obstacle is not simply finding work. It is finding a job that offers reliable income, stability and a path towards independence.

If economic expansion fails to create enough productive jobs, its benefits will remain limited for large sections of the population.

Chkoundali identifies weak investment and declining production as major constraints. He also warns that the government’s reliance on domestic borrowing could make it harder for private businesses to obtain financing, expand and hire.

According to figures he cited, domestic borrowing amounted to about 7 billion dinars ($2.3bn) in both 2024 and 2025, with 11 billion dinars ($3.7bn) in borrowing at the beginning of 2026.

The concern is that the state’s financing needs could compete with private businesses for available credit. Domestic borrowing does not automatically undermine growth; its effects depend on the terms of financing and how the money is spent. But if businesses struggle to secure funds for investment, the consequences can be felt in production and employment.

Tunisia faces a difficult balancing act: financing the state’s obligations while creating conditions for private enterprise to grow and provide jobs.

For workers such as Oueslati, the consequences are immediate. When operating costs rise but earnings do not keep pace, longer hours can become a way of standing still rather than moving ahead.

The fight against speculation

Saied has made combating monopolies and speculation a central part of his economic agenda, presenting the campaign as a way to protect consumers, curb abusive practices and advance social justice.

The objective speaks to public frustration over rising prices. But critics argue that the authorities have not always adequately distinguished between speculative stockpiling and the storage necessary to keep essential goods available.

Warehousing, inventory management and distribution are integral to functioning supply chains. Restrictions that disrupt these systems without providing alternatives can, critics warn, contribute to shortages rather than bring prices down.

The risk is particularly significant in markets that depend on imports and distribution networks operated by private companies and public-sector entities. When stocks run low or supply channels are disrupted, goods can become harder to find even when government intervention is intended to protect consumers.

Enforcement may be necessary to tackle abusive practices, but it cannot replace the infrastructure and commercial systems needed to keep goods moving.

Protecting consumers therefore requires more than confronting speculation. It also requires policies that preserve reliable supplies, support production and ensure essential goods reach the market.

In a statement, the Democratic Current party criticised what it described as a refusal to confront economic realities, arguing that attributing failures to conspiracies would deepen the country’s problems rather than resolve them.

The government’s interventions must ultimately be judged by their results. A policy designed to protect consumers must be assessed not only by its stated purpose, but also by its effects on prices and availability of goods.

Debt and the limits of public spending

The government faces another constraint in its efforts to support economic activity and shield households from rising costs: The burden of financing the state.

Tunisia’s public debt rose from 67.8% of gross domestic product in 2019 to 84.9% in 2024, before falling to 82.1% in 2025, according to Finance Ministry data. The 2026 Finance Law projects a ratio of approximately 83.4%.

Debt levels alone do not determine whether public finances are sustainable. Borrowing costs, repayment schedules, government revenue and economic growth also matter. But substantial financing needs can leave the state with less flexibility to respond to new shocks.

Debt servicing competes with public-sector wages, social spending, subsidies and investment. The government must meet existing obligations while funding services and projects that could strengthen the economy over the longer term.

Chkoundali argues that the state’s financing needs have narrowed its options. The question is not simply how much the government borrows, but whether its financing choices leave enough resources for productive investment.

That pressure becomes more acute when international energy prices rise.

The cost of shielding consumers from oil prices

Tunisia’s 2026 Finance Law assumed a Brent crude price of about $63.30 per barrel. By the end of June, the average price had reached approximately $92.60, according to figures cited in the report.

The increase raised the potential cost of energy imports and fuel subsidies, putting additional pressure on public finances.

Fuel subsidies amounted to 2.427 billion dinars in the first half of 2026, equivalent to $826m. That represented 48.6% of the allocation for fuel subsidies under the Finance Law.

Public investment expenditure over the same period totalled 1.665 billion dinars, or approximately $566.6m.

The figures show how the government must balance competing demands on the budget. Subsidies shield consumers from some of the immediate effects of higher energy prices. But when oil costs more than expected, maintaining that protection becomes more expensive, potentially leaving fewer resources for public investment.

Cutting subsidies too abruptly could transfer more of the burden to households and businesses. Maintaining them, meanwhile, can intensify fiscal pressure when international prices rise sharply.

The consequences may extend beyond government spending. A larger energy import bill increases demand for foreign currency and may put pressure on the dinar and foreign-exchange reserves, particularly if export earnings and domestic production fail to offset the additional costs.

Chkoundali also points to trade imbalances involving partners including Algeria and Egypt as part of the wider external challenge.

He argues that policymakers should prepare multiple scenarios when estimating financing needs and subsidy costs, rather than rely on a single oil-price forecast. Such planning could help the government anticipate market changes before they place unexpected strain on the budget.

For Tunisia, the challenge is to shield households from external shocks without undermining the investment needed to make the economy more productive and less vulnerable to them.

What did Saied inherit?

Saied’s supporters argue that his economic record cannot be assessed without considering the problems that preceded his presidency.

Houssam Ben Ahmed, a political activist who supports the president, says Saied inherited a country already in serious decline across several sectors. He describes the measures taken on July 25, 2021 as “an absolute necessity to save the state”, citing what he sees as the fragmentation and deterioration of political and economic life.

From this perspective, the disruption that followed was part of a confrontation with longstanding problems, rather than evidence that Saied’s policies alone were responsible for the country’s difficulties.

The argument points to an important distinction in assessing any government’s economic record. The pandemic, international market volatility and geopolitical tensions have affected Tunisia, while structural weaknesses and political disputes long predate Saied’s presidency.

But inherited problems and external shocks do not remove the need to examine the decisions made in office. They form part of the context against which the government’s choices and results must be judged.

Has the government improved conditions for investment? Has it strengthened domestic production, created jobs and protected living standards? And where improvements have occurred, have they been sufficient to meet public expectations?

Supporters emphasise the difficulties Saied inherited. Critics point to persistent pressure on household budgets and limited opportunities for young people. A meaningful assessment must look beyond both claims to the evidence: What has improved, what has deteriorated and how much can reasonably be attributed to government policy?

The test of economic progress

Nearly seven years into Saied’s presidency, Tunisia’s economic record remains mixed. The economy continues to grow, and overall unemployment has eased from its pandemic-era peak. Yet food prices remain high, joblessness among young people persists, and public finances face competing demands.

External shocks have made recovery harder. But enduring a crisis is not the same as emerging from it. An economy can weather successive shocks without delivering the improvements in income, employment and security that people expect.

A more convincing recovery would mean stronger productive investment, more stable jobs, higher domestic production and incomes that keep pace with the cost of living. It would also require the government to manage its financing needs without sacrificing the investment on which future growth depends.

For Oueslati, the debate comes down to the cost of keeping his taxi on the road. Every increase in operating expenses eats into his earnings. Every additional hour behind the wheel is time spent trying to make up the difference.

One driver’s experience cannot determine the success or failure of an entire economic programme. But it highlights what national statistics can obscure: Whether people can turn their work into a more secure standard of living.

For Oueslati, progress would mean being able to keep his taxi on the road without having to work ever longer hours simply to make ends meet.

entries.title: White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny
entries.summary: Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed to be a lawyer, but critics question whether she was ever licensed.
entries.content:
Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed to be a lawyer, but critics question if she passed the bar exam to be licensed.

Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary under United States President Donald Trump, has drawn increasing criticism over claims about her professional background.

On Wednesday, a public accountability nonprofit filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over Zacharia’s repeated claims that she was a lawyer.

If made falsely, such a claim is a crime in the state. According to Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile, she received a degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but critics have questioned whether she received a licence to practise law, as she has suggested.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the head of the Washington, DC-based Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement. “Yet it seems it was all a lie.”

Her organisation filed the complaint with California’s bar office, a regulatory agency that oversees the licensing of lawyers.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” Kuppersmith said.

“The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

Zacharia, a commentator who has appeared frequently on Fox News and Newsmax, began her term as White House press secretary on Tuesday.

In a news briefing that day, she seemed to falter and speak haltingly, sometimes having to repeat herself.

Her appearance was brief, lasting under 15 minutes. She spent much of her time at the podium thanking Trump for the opportunity and reading from a prepared statement.

“I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia said.

Later, she joined Trump outside the White House to speak further with reporters. When asked where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.”

The response was an apparent reference to a three-year stint in which she claims she worked at a law firm in Beijing.

A biography on the website for the pro-Trump women’s organisation Trumpettes USA Inc says she “served as outside counsel” for the World Bank and International Finance Corporation while in Beijing.

Her LinkedIn profile, meanwhile, indicates Zacharia served as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. More recently, from 2024 to 2025, it lists her as general counsel for Fix California, a voter rights group started by a Trump administration official.

On her Instagram profile, Zacharia describes herself as a “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer”.

But Zacharia’s assertion that she passed the bar in China has fuelled media scrutiny. China’s equivalent of the bar exam, the notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination, can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

China has, on rare occasion, allowed foreigners to practise law in the country if they have several years of experience in their home countries first.

But that does not appear to be the case for Zacharia. According to media reports, Zacharia has not been found to be licensed as a lawyer in any state in the US.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Zacharia responded to the scrutiny by saying, “I practice international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”

Since Trump’s return to office for a second term, Zacharia has spent several months as a communications adviser at the Department of Homeland Security.

Since June, she has also worked as the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform.

entries.title: Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
entries.summary: The US president has long been unhappy with inside information about his administration being leaked to the media.
entries.content:
The US president has long been unhappy with inside information about his administration being leaked to the media.

United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.

Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.

In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.

That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.

It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.

Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.

“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.

“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”

Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.

After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.

“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”

Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.

Staff in his administration, as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.

Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.

The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.

Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.

Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.

Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.

Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.

Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.

“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

entries.title: Istanbul in chaos, shut down by heaviest rainfall since 1985
entries.summary: Torrential rain has triggered flash floods across Istanbul.
entries.content:
Istanbul in chaos, shut down by heaviest rainfall since 1985

NewsFeed

Istanbul in chaos, shut down by heaviest rainfall since 1985

Torrential rain has triggered flash floods across Istanbul. The downpour swept cars through neighbourhoods, stranded people, triggered landslides and brought traffic to a standstill, with more rain to come.

Published On 15 Oct 2026

entries.title: Ship catches fire in Romania’s waters amid rising attacks in the Black Sea
entries.summary: Authorities are investigating whether drones may have been involved in the latest incident.
entries.content:
Authorities are investigating whether drones may have been involved in the latest incident.

A ship anchored in Romania’s territorial waters has caught fire and the crew has been evacuated, Romanian authorities said.

The incident comes amid growing concerns over hybrid attacks in the Black Sea involving Russia.

Romanian Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Wednesday it was unclear whether a drone had hit the ship, identified as the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, and that an investigation was pending.

Multiple drones breached Romanian airspace on Wednesday near its border with Ukraine.

On Tuesday, two ships were hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

Radev said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident.

Earlier shipping attacks

Earlier this month, a grain ship caught fire and sank outside Romania’s territorial waters. Ukraine blamed Russian drones for the incident, in which two people were killed and 11 others rescued.

“A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkiye,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

Some see incursions by Russian drones into eastern European airspace as a test of NATO and the European Union’s defences and response capabilities.

Romania, a NATO member, shares a land border with Ukraine. Since the Russia-Ukraine war started, drones have breached its airspace while mines floating in the Black Sea threaten key trade and energy routes.

Last Wednesday, Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova said she would invite Romania and Turkiye to consultations on ensuring the security of merchant ships in the Black Sea.

On October 6, two ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One sank and the other was damaged.

The crew of the damaged ship were rescued, but the crew of the sunken one remain missing. Bulgarian authorities ended search operations after confirming no survivors were found.

entries.title: Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
entries.summary: President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of 'tough-on-crime model' embraced by her government.
entries.content:
President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of ‘tough-on-crime model’ embraced by her government.

Costa Rica has announced the opening of a new mega-prison amid near-record homicide levels and growing organised crime, as countries across the region embrace police crackdowns that have proven popular but often weaken key civil liberties.

President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime, or CACCO, on Wednesday. The prison will have capacity for 5,100 people, equivalent to about 20 percent of the country’s current prison population.

“The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during an inauguration ceremony.

Candidates across Latin America have embraced mega-prisons, seeking to replicate the policies of Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador, who has won widespread popularity through a campaign of mass arrests and the suspension of basic rights in the name of combating crime.

Costa Rica, long spared from high levels of violent crime compared with its neighbours, saw a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.

Analysts say that is partly due to increased fighting between criminal groups over lucrative drug routes.

The first transfers to Costa Rica’s new mega-prison will take place at the end of October, with Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar saying the facility will help the government reassert control over the prison system and diminish infiltration by organised crime.

Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated in July, has announced plans to tour El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), in anticipation of creating a similar facility in her country. CECOT can hold about 40,000 people.

In Colombia, meanwhile, newly elected leader Abelardo de la Espriella campaigned for the presidency, in part, on a pledge to build 10 mega-prisons. He took office in August.

Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, is currently in the midst of its own presidential election, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has advanced to the final round of the vote. His platform also includes building five mega-prisons, citing the Salvadoran model.

El Salvador first imposed a “state of exception” under Bukele in 2022, expanding police and military powers.

That emergency declaration has been credited with a sharp drop in that country’s homicides, but rights groups say it has led to severe rights abuses and has been weaponised against critics of the government.

The “state of exception” has also resulted in mass arrests and mass trials, with rulings delivered against hundreds of defendants at a time. Some defendants have been detained without charge.

While the Bukele administration frequently touts its success in dismantling the gangs, the government has continuously extended the state of exception since it was first imposed.

Critics have warned that conditions inside mega-prisons are often poor, with imprisoned people facing overcrowding, due process violations and alleged torture in facilities like CECOT.

entries.title: Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
entries.summary: Victims' groups, however, have denounced the ruling as 'selective' justice that exonerates the former migration chief.
entries.content:
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.

A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.

The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.

Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.

On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.

“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.

The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.

In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.

Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.

On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.

As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.

Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.

Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.

The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.

Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.

Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.

In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.

Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

The US says it destroyed an Iran-affiliated boat in the Gulf of Oman, accusing it of conducting surveillance and targeting US naval forces in the strategic waterway. The US says all crew members were taken off the dhow when it was intercepted and destroyed on October 6th.
